Lesson Overview

In your last lesson, you meticulously refined your mousetrap car — testing variables, gathering data, and making informed decisions to push your car's performance as far as it could go. Now you've arrived at a pivotal moment: the final runs. This is where all of that hard work comes together in a definitive demonstration of what your car can really do.

Today's lesson also introduces the Creationeering™ phase of Death & Recycling. Every engineered design has a life cycle — a beginning, a period of use, and eventually an end. You'll conduct your final performance tests, analyze your complete data set, and then reflect on what happens when a design reaches the end of its intended use. More importantly, you'll think about how the lessons learned — and even the materials themselves — can be recycled and repurposed for future, even better, creations.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Conduct accurate final performance tests of your mousetrap car, following established procedures.
  • Collect and systematically record all necessary data from your car's final runs.
  • Analyze your collected data to evaluate overall performance and identify areas of success and potential improvement.
  • Apply the Creationeering™ Death & Recycling phase by reflecting on your car's life cycle and potential for future iterations.
  • Connect responsible stewardship of materials and knowledge to honoring God's intricate designs in creation.

items.definition: The conclusive performance test of a completed engineering design, used to gather definitive data on its capabilities.
The process of inspecting, transforming, and modeling data to discover useful information and support decision-making.
The decline in a system's efficiency or effectiveness over time due to wear, fatigue, or other factors.
In Creationeering™, the phase where a product's life cycle ends and its components or design principles are considered for reuse, repurposing, or improvement in new designs.
Analyzing a system by connecting observations at a large scale (macro) to causes at a very small scale (atomic or molecular).
The responsible overseeing and protection of something considered worth caring for and preserving.
A repetition of a process or series of steps, often with the aim of improving a design or solution.
A situation where gaining one quality or aspect of a design means losing another quality or aspect.

data.html:
From Dust to Dust: The Life Cycle of Creation

Everything in creation has a life cycle — a beginning, a season of purpose, and an end that often seeds something new. The sun rises and sets. Rivers flow to the sea and return through the water cycle. Seasons come and go. This isn't random; it's a beautifully designed pattern woven into the fabric of creation by God Himself.

Your mousetrap car follows that same pattern. It was born as raw materials and an idea. It was built, tested, refined, and improved. Now it runs its final laps. And when those runs are complete, the design doesn't simply disappear — the knowledge you gained, the mistakes you learned from, and even the physical components can be transformed into something new. That's the heart of the Death & Recycling phase.

Ecclesiastes 1:4–7 (KJV) — "One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth abideth for ever. The sun also ariseth, and the sun goeth down, and hasteth to his place where he arose. The wind goeth toward the south, and turneth about unto the north; it whirleth about continually, and the wind returneth again according to his circuits. All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea is not full; unto the place from whence the rivers come, thither they return again."

These cycles aren't accidents — they're God's engineering at work. Just as He built renewal into creation, He invites you to build renewal into your designs.

Conducting Your Final Runs

A final run is different from an optimization test. During optimization, you were changing things — adjusting axle positions, swapping wheels, tweaking the string length. Now you're done making changes. The car is locked in. Your job is simply to measure what it can do as accurately and consistently as possible.

Think of it like a product launch. An engineer doesn't keep redesigning a bridge after it opens to traffic. At some point, the design is finalized and performance is officially recorded. That's exactly what you're doing today.

Before You Run: Pre-Test Checklist

Before your car rolls an inch, take a few minutes to verify the following:

  • All components are securely fastened — no loose wheels, axles, or string.
  • The mousetrap spring is in its starting position and the lever arm is set correctly.
  • Your measurement tools are ready: a measuring tape or meter stick and a timer if you're recording speed.
  • Your data table is prepared and ready to fill in — don't rely on memory.

data.caption: A student placing a mousetrap car at the starting line on a smooth floor, with a measuring tape extended along the path of travel and a data recording sheet nearby

data.html:
Running the Test

Conduct a minimum of three final runs. Three runs give you enough data to spot a pattern and calculate an average — one run alone could be an outlier, either surprisingly great or surprisingly poor. Consistency is what you're really measuring.

For each run, record:

  • Distance traveled — measure from the starting line to where the car stops (front of the car).
  • Time — if you're measuring speed, use a consistent start and stop point every run.
  • Observations — did the car drift left or right? Did the string release cleanly? Any unusual sounds or behaviors?

Keep your starting position identical for every run. Even a small difference in how the car is placed can change your results — and that's a variable you don't want to introduce at this stage.

Don't skip the qualitative observations. Numbers tell you what happened, but your written observations tell you why. If your third run is shorter than your first two, a note like "string slipped off the axle slightly" explains the drop. That insight is just as valuable as the distance measurement.

Analyzing Your Data

Once all your runs are complete, the real engineering work begins: making sense of what the numbers actually mean. Raw data is just a list of measurements. Data analysis is how you turn that list into understanding.

Calculate Your Average

Add up all your distance measurements and divide by the number of runs. This is your mean distance — the best single number to represent your car's typical performance. If you also recorded time, calculate your average time the same way, then use it to find average speed:

Speed = Distance ÷ Time

Look for Patterns

Were your runs consistent, or did performance drop over time? A drop in distance across consecutive runs is a classic sign of performance degradation — the spring losing a bit of energy with each use, or friction increasing as components wear. Noticing this pattern is the kind of insight that separates a careful engineer from someone who just collected numbers.

Compare to Your Optimization Data

Pull out your data from the optimization tests in the previous lesson. Did your final design actually perform better than your earlier versions? Did any of your changes backfire? Comparing across time is one of the most powerful things you can do with data — it's how engineers prove that their improvements actually worked.

data.caption: A hand-drawn or printed data table showing three final run distances, the calculated average, and a simple bar chart comparing the three runs side by side

data.html:
The Death & Recycling Phase

Here's the part of engineering that doesn't get talked about enough: what comes after the final test. In Creationeering™, the Death & Recycling phase recognizes that every design eventually reaches the end of its intended use — and that ending is not a failure. It's a doorway.

Think about how God designed the natural world. A fallen tree doesn't just disappear; it becomes soil, habitat, and nutrients for new growth. A dying star scatters heavy elements across the galaxy that eventually become part of new planets. Nothing is truly wasted in God's creation — it's transformed.

Your mousetrap car works the same way. When this project is complete, consider:

  • Materials recycling — Can the wood, wheels, axles, or springs be salvaged and used in your next build?
  • Knowledge recycling — What did you learn about friction, leverage, and energy transfer that you'll apply immediately in future projects?
  • Design recycling — Which features of this car worked so well that they should become your starting point next time, not something you have to rediscover?

The best engineers don't start from scratch. They build on what came before. That's not laziness — it's wisdom. It's stewardship of the knowledge and resources God has already given you.

Trade-offs and What They Teach You

As you reflect on your final data, you'll likely notice that your car was great at some things and not others. Maybe it traveled a long distance but wasn't very straight. Maybe it was fast but inconsistent. These aren't mistakes — they're trade-offs.

Every engineering design involves trade-offs. A car built for maximum distance might use a longer lever arm, which slows initial acceleration. A car optimized for speed might sacrifice distance. Recognizing the trade-offs in your own design is a sign that your engineering thinking has matured. You now understand that there's rarely a perfect solution — just the best solution for a specific goal.

Ask yourself: What was my primary goal for this car? How well did my design serve that goal? And what would I trade differently if I built it again? Those three questions are the foundation of every engineering reflection.

Write your reflection while the details are fresh. Right after your final runs, spend five minutes jotting down what worked, what didn't, and what you'd change. Future-you will be grateful — and if you ever build another mousetrap car, those notes are worth more than any textbook.

Stewardship: Honoring God with Your Work

Stewardship isn't just about taking care of physical materials — though that matters too. It's about taking care of everything God has entrusted to you: your time, your talents, your knowledge, and yes, your supplies. When you carefully disassemble your mousetrap car and sort which parts can be reused, you're practicing stewardship. When you write down your lessons learned instead of letting them fade, you're practicing stewardship. When you share what worked with a classmate who's still struggling, you're practicing stewardship.

God is the ultimate engineer and designer, and He designed creation to be cared for — not used up and discarded. Your mousetrap car project is a small but real opportunity to mirror that same care in your own work. How you finish a project says just as much about your character as how you start it.

data.title: Going Deeper: Multiscale Modeling and Why Materials Wear Out
data.html:
When your mousetrap car's performance degrades after several runs, what's actually happening? On the surface, it looks like the spring is getting weaker or the wheels are spinning less freely. But zoom in to the microscopic level and you'd see something fascinating: the metal in the spring is experiencing tiny structural changes as it flexes repeatedly, and the contact surfaces between axles and supports are developing microscopic scratches that increase friction.

This is the idea behind multiscale modeling — connecting what you see happening at the large scale (your car slowing down) to causes at the very small scale (material fatigue and surface wear). Real engineers use multiscale modeling to predict how long materials will last, when a bridge needs maintenance, or why a jet engine component might fail after a certain number of flight cycles.

You experienced multiscale modeling intuitively every time you noticed performance degradation and tried to diagnose why. That instinct — to ask "what's really going on at a deeper level?" — is exactly the mindset that makes great engineers.

Wrapping It Up

You've done something genuinely impressive. You took a raw idea, built it with your own hands, tested it, improved it through careful iteration, and now you've run it for the final time with the data to prove what it can do. That's the full engineering design cycle — not as a classroom exercise, but as a real process that mirrors what engineers do every day in the world.

The mousetrap car project doesn't end with your final run. It ends when you've captured your data, reflected on your trade-offs, honored the materials by considering how they can be reused, and carried your hard-won knowledge into whatever you build next. That's the Death & Recycling phase in action — and it's one of the most important habits you can build as an engineer and as a steward of what God has given you.

Well done. Now go run those final laps.
